surveyed_by: research task, owner work order #2 and #5
purpose: Compare candidate sources of daily historical prices that include delisted, bankrupt and acquired securities, so a human can decide whether a paid dependency is justified. NOTHING WAS PURCHASED, REGISTERED FOR, OR AUTHENTICATED TO. Every claim below was read from public documentation, a public pricing page, or measured locally; the verification field says which.
requirement: daily bars for securities that no longer trade (delisted, bankrupt, acquired, taken private)
the delisting/terminal event and, where one exists, a real terminal price -- never an invented one
corporate actions: splits, dividends, spin-offs, mergers, bankruptcies
a permanent security identifier that survives ticker reuse and renaming
RAW AS-TRADED prices retrievable, not only back-adjusted ones: point-in-time share counts are pre-split, so a point-in-time market cap needs an unadjusted price
a licence that permits building a commercial product, or a clear statement that it does not

verification_vocabulary.measured_locally: observed by running code against local files, the local store, or a public endpoint during this survey
verification_vocabulary.vendor_page: read from the vendor's own public page during this survey
verification_vocabulary.vendor_doc: read from the vendor's own public API documentation during this survey
verification_vocabulary.third_party: read from a non-vendor source (review, integrator, search summary); weaker
verification_vocabulary.not_verified: could not be read without signing up or the page did not load; recorded as UNKNOWN

sources.name: Yahoo Finance chart API (what the store uses today)
sources.delisted_coverage: NONE. Measured 2026-09-21: the v8 chart endpoint returned HTTP 404 for all seven dead tickers probed (AVP acquired 2020, X acquired 2025, BBBYQ Ch.11 stub, SHLDQ Ch.11 stub, LEHMQ, TWTR taken private 2022, CBS merged 2019) and full history for the live control AAPL. Not a gap in history -- the symbol ceases to exist.
sources.earliest_date: 1962 for long-lived survivors (measured: DIS, ED, IBM, JNJ, KO, XRX all begin 1962-01-02)
sources.corporate_actions: div and split events on the chart endpoint for LIVE names only; no merger, spin-off or bankruptcy terminal event
sources.permanent_identifiers: none -- ticker only, and tickers are reused
sources.adjustment_methodology: back-adjusted close (auto_adjust) plus a raw close field; adjustment silently rewrites the whole history on each new action
sources.api_format: JSON over HTTPS, one symbol per call
sources.licensing: no commercial licence; personal use at the vendor's sufferance
sources.cost_evidence: no charge
sources.integration_complexity: already integrated (pit_listing 2,574 rows, pit_price_bar 9,305,417 bars)
sources.caveats: This is the whole problem. The 2,574-listing sample is survivor-only by construction, so every return result from it is SURVIVOR_ONLY_DIAGNOSTIC.

sources.name: CRSP US Stock Database (Center for Research in Security Prices; acquired by Morningstar 2026-02-02)
sources.delisted_coverage: YES, and it is the reference standard. Vendor page: 'more than 36,000 active and inactive securities'. Carries DLSTDT (delist date), DLSTCD (delist code, e.g. 574 = delisted by exchange, bankruptcy/insolvency) and DLRET (delisting return).
sources.earliest_date: vendor page: 'over 100 years' (CRSP daily data is conventionally 1925-12-31 forward; monthly earlier)
sources.corporate_actions: full: distributions, splits, exchanges, mergers, delisting events, share-count history
sources.permanent_identifiers: PERMNO -- vendor page: 'a proprietary, permanent identifier ... Fixed for the life of a security'; also PERMCO, plus CUSIP history and a CIK link
sources.adjustment_methodology: raw as-traded prices with separate cumulative adjustment factors (CFACPR/CFACSHR) and returns computed by CRSP; the user chooses adjusted or not
sources.unadjusted_retrievable: yes -- this is CRSP's native form
sources.api_format: flat files (CIZ format 2.0), CRSPAccess, WRDS SAS/SQL/cloud query, R/Python via WRDS
sources.licensing: vendor page: 'designed for and delivered to licensees at academic institutions, government agencies, and investment practitioners'. Redistribution is contractually restricted; building a commercial product on it requires a practitioner licence negotiated with CRSP/Morningstar.
sources.cost_evidence: no public price. CRSP directs to subscriptions@crsp.ChicagoBooth.edu. Academic-institution access is normally via a university WRDS subscription, which an individual cannot buy.
sources.integration_complexity: high: flat-file ingest is mechanically easy (stdlib csv), but access is the problem -- no self-serve API key, and the licence is the gate, not the format
sources.caveats: Even CRSP has MISSING delisting returns for some names; researchers substitute values from similar delistings. Under owner rule 4 we would keep those as OUTCOME_UNKNOWN rather than adopt the academic substitution convention.

sources.name: LSEG (Refinitiv) DataScope Select / DataScope Plus
sources.delisted_coverage: YES. Vendor material describes access to on the order of 80 million active and retired instruments across asset classes.
sources.delisted_from: UNKNOWN (not stated on the public fact sheets read)
sources.corporate_actions: yes, corporate actions are a first-class product line
sources.permanent_identifiers: PermID, RIC history, SEDOL/ISIN/CUSIP cross-reference
sources.adjustment_methodology: UNKNOWN in detail; both adjusted and unadjusted series are normally available
sources.api_format: scheduled/on-demand file extraction (SFTP, REST), fixed-format or CSV
sources.licensing: negotiated; redistribution and commercial product rights are separately priced
sources.cost_evidence: no public price; third-party marketplace listings quote order-of-thousands per user per month, which is not a vendor statement
sources.integration_complexity: high: entitlement, extraction templates and an account manager before a single byte arrives
sources.caveats: Priced for institutions; no self-serve path for a one-person research project.

sources.name: Bloomberg Data License (B-PIPE / Data License, not the Terminal)
sources.delisted_coverage: yes for delisted equities via historical Data License requests
sources.corporate_actions: yes, a dedicated corporate-actions product
sources.permanent_identifiers: BBGID / FIGI, plus Bloomberg tickers with exchange suffixes
sources.adjustment_methodology: both adjusted and unadjusted are available in the Terminal/API model
sources.unadjusted_retrievable: UNKNOWN in the Data License context
sources.api_format: Data License request/response files, B-PIPE, BLPAPI
sources.licensing: the most restrictive of the set: per-application entitlement, explicit prohibition on redistribution, commercial use negotiated
sources.cost_evidence: Terminal list pricing is widely reported around $30k/user/year; Data License is priced separately and is not published. Treat any specific number as unverified.
sources.integration_complexity: high
sources.caveats: Out of proportion to this project by an order of magnitude.

sources.name: FactSet Prices + FactSet Symbology
sources.delisted_coverage: yes; FactSet symbology carries inactive securities and the entity/security mapping over time
sources.corporate_actions: yes
sources.permanent_identifiers: FactSet permanent identifiers (FSYM regional/security/entity ids)
sources.adjustment_methodology: adjusted and unadjusted available
sources.api_format: REST APIs, Standard DataFeed (bulk files), Snowflake share
sources.licensing: negotiated; quote-based, no published list price
sources.cost_evidence: FactSet publishes no list price; third-party buyer guides cite five-figure annual medians. Not vendor-verified.
sources.integration_complexity: high

sources.name: S&P Capital IQ / Compustat Security Daily
sources.delisted_coverage: yes; Compustat retains inactive issues (the research 'Compustat North America - Security Daily' file covers delisted names, and CIQ carries the transaction history)
sources.earliest_date: Compustat annual fundamentals from 1950; Security Daily prices later (UNKNOWN exact)
sources.corporate_actions: yes
sources.permanent_identifiers: GVKEY (company) + IID (issue); CIQ companyId/tradingItemId
sources.adjustment_methodology: raw price plus adjustment factor (AJEXDI), so both forms are derivable
sources.api_format: WRDS, Xpressfeed bulk load, Snowflake, APIs
sources.licensing: negotiated; academic access via WRDS institutional subscription
sources.cost_evidence: no public price
sources.integration_complexity: high (Xpressfeed is a loader-shaped product, not a file you read with stdlib)
sources.caveats: Compustat's own delisting metadata is weaker than CRSP's; the standard research practice is CRSP for prices/delisting returns and Compustat for fundamentals.

sources.name: Norgate Data - US Stocks (Platinum / Diamond)
sources.delisted_coverage: YES, prominently. Third-party review cites 25,222 delisted securities in the database. Delisted symbols are suffixed -YYYYMM, the year and month of the last trading day, so a reused ticker cannot collide with its dead predecessor.
sources.earliest_date: Platinum 1990, Diamond 1950 (vendor packages page); a third-party review notes coverage is effectively complete from late 1992
sources.corporate_actions: NOT delivered as discrete events. Vendor FAQ: corporate actions are incorporated into the price series through the chosen adjustment method. That is a real limitation for us -- we want the EVENT in pit_corporate_action, not only its effect.
sources.permanent_identifiers: assetid -- vendor FAQ: 'a static, stable, unchanging, non-recycled, unique identifier for each security' surviving symbol changes
sources.adjustment_methodology: four selectable modes: unadjusted (raw), adjusted for capital reconstructions, capital reconstructions + special distributions, and total return (ordinary dividends included)
sources.api_format: Windows 'Norgate Data Updater' application writing a proprietary local database, consumed via the norgatedata Python package or AmiBroker/Zipline plugins
sources.licensing: single-user subscription; redistribution not permitted. Commercial-product rights UNKNOWN from the public pages and would need to be asked.
sources.cost_evidence: vendor packages page as read 2026-09-21: Silver $270/yr (10y, no delisted), Gold $360/yr (20y, no delisted), Platinum $630/yr (1990, delisted included), Diamond $787.50/yr (1950, delisted included)
sources.integration_complexity: high for THIS architecture: the delivery path is a Windows desktop updater plus a Python package that depends on pandas/numpy, which the stdlib-only rule forbids. A stdlib ingest would have to read the package's exported CSV, not the native store.
sources.caveats: Best price-per-dollar for delisted US equities, but discrete corporate-action events and terminal-value-per-share are not exposed, and 25,222 delisted names at ~2,500 bars each would be roughly 7.7 GB in pit_price_bar at the measured 121.8 bytes/bar -- more than the 11 GB free on this volume once WAL is counted.

sources.name: Sharadar Equity Prices (SEP) + TICKERS + ACTIONS, via Nasdaq Data Link or the new Sharadar Direct
sources.delisted_coverage: YES, explicitly. Vendor: 'The data includes active and delisted securities, minimizing survivorship bias' and 'nearly completely free of survivorship bias', 'point-in-time ready'.
sources.earliest_date: December 1997 / 1998 depending on the page; ~21,000 tickers
sources.corporate_actions: YES as discrete events -- a separate ACTIONS table (dividends, splits, spin-offs, mergers, bankruptcies, ticker changes) alongside the price table
sources.permanent_identifiers: permaticker (a permanent integer id that survives ticker changes) plus CIK cross-reference in the TICKERS table; that table also carries firstpricedate/lastpricedate and an isdelisted flag
sources.adjustment_methodology: three parallel forms in one row: unadjusted close (closeunadj), split-adjusted OHLCV, and split+dividend+spin-off adjusted close (closeadj)
sources.unadjusted_retrievable: YES -- closeunadj is a named field
sources.api_format: REST JSON/CSV plus bulk CSV export of the whole table; also SQLite/Postgres/Sheets integrations
sources.licensing: two-tier: non-professional (personal) vs professional. Professionals must buy through Nasdaq Data Link. Redistribution is not permitted on either; a commercial product built on it needs the professional licence and probably a conversation.
sources.cost_category: UNKNOWN (public pages require a login to display the number; historically low hundreds to low thousands per year depending on professional status)
sources.cost_evidence: Nasdaq Data Link help page confirms prices are only shown after account-type selection/login. NOT PRICED HERE -- do not quote a number without checking.
sources.integration_complexity: LOW, and the best fit of the set: flat CSV + REST JSON, parseable with stdlib csv/json/urllib; permaticker maps cleanly onto pit_listing.listing_id semantics; ACTIONS maps onto pit_corporate_action including terminal events; closeunadj satisfies the pre-split share-count requirement
sources.caveats: History starts ~1998, so it cannot reach a 1990s replay -- irrelevant here: our peer sets start 2013-01-31 and our bars start 2011-01-03. Sharadar is a fundamentals-first vendor; price quality for thin OTC stubs after a Chapter 11 is UNKNOWN and would need a sample check.

sources.name: EOD Historical Data (EODHD)
sources.delisted_coverage: Claimed: EOD, fundamentals, news and intraday for delisted companies; delisted tickers are exposed through the Exchange API and marked with an '_old' suffix (e.g. ACR_old.US) once the live ticker is reused.
sources.delisted_from: UNKNOWN; the vendor states requests outside a security's trading life return nothing
sources.corporate_actions: splits and dividends endpoints; merger/bankruptcy terminal events UNKNOWN
sources.permanent_identifiers: none permanent -- the '_old' suffix is a collision workaround, not an identifier; CIK/ISIN present in fundamentals
sources.adjustment_methodology: close plus adjusted_close
sources.api_format: REST JSON/CSV, bulk end-of-day download per exchange per day
sources.licensing: personal use on the standard plans; vendor states commercial use requires the Startups & Enterprise plan
sources.cost_evidence: vendor pricing page as read 2026-09-21: EOD All World $19.99/mo or $199/yr; EOD+Intraday $29.99/mo; Fundamentals $59.99/mo; ALL-IN-ONE $99.99/mo or $999.90/yr. Commercial tier is quote-based.
sources.integration_complexity: low: REST + CSV, stdlib-compatible
sources.caveats: The delisted claim is not backed by a published coverage count or a delisting-date field on the public pages. Their own FAQ hedges: data exists only for the traded period. Quality of the dead tail is unproven -- it would need a sample test against known 2013-2020 delistings before it could replace anything.

sources.name: Polygon.io (polygon.io now 301-redirects to massive.com)
sources.delisted_coverage: YES for reference data: the tickers endpoint takes active=false and returns delisted_utc, 'the last date that the asset was traded'. Historical aggregates for those symbols are available on paid tiers.
sources.delisted_from: reference history back to 2003-09-10 on paid tiers (Basic: 2 years)
sources.corporate_actions: splits and dividends endpoints; 'Corporate Actions' listed on every tier. Merger/bankruptcy terminal events UNKNOWN.
sources.permanent_identifiers: CIK and composite FIGI are returned. CUSIP is queryable but NOT returned, for licensing reasons.
sources.adjustment_methodology: aggregates take an adjusted=true/false parameter
sources.unadjusted_retrievable: YES -- adjusted=false is a first-class parameter
sources.api_format: REST JSON plus S3-style flat files on paid tiers
sources.licensing: self-serve; commercial use permitted on business tiers, redistribution restricted; exchange-data rules apply to real-time, less so to EOD history
sources.cost_evidence: pricing page as read 2026-09-21: Stocks Basic free (2y), Starter $29/mo (5y), Developer $79/mo (10y), Advanced $199/mo (20y+, flat files, financials)
sources.integration_complexity: low: REST JSON + flat files, stdlib-compatible; the delisted_utc field maps directly onto a pit_listing.valid_to and an OUTCOME_UNKNOWN-or-not decision
sources.caveats: History begins 2003, fine for our 2011+ bars. The brand migration to massive.com happened recently enough that continuity of terms should be re-checked before committing. Whether the aggregates for a delisted symbol are complete to its final session is UNKNOWN and must be sample-tested.

sources.name: Tiingo
sources.delisted_coverage: UNKNOWN. The pricing page advertises 110,044 securities and '30+ years' of price history but says nothing about delisted names or survivorship bias.
sources.corporate_actions: splits and dividend fields on the EOD endpoint
sources.permanent_identifiers: none published
sources.adjustment_methodology: adjusted and raw OHLC both returned on the EOD endpoint
sources.api_format: REST JSON/CSV
sources.licensing: restrictive on the cheap tier -- vendor: 'Internal use means you may only use the data for your own personal use and you may not display or share the data with another person or organization.' Commercial licensing is contact-sales.
sources.cost_evidence: pricing page as read 2026-09-21: Starter $0, Power $30/mo
sources.integration_complexity: low
sources.caveats: Cannot be recommended for this requirement without a published delisted-coverage statement. Do not assume.

sources.name: Intrinio
sources.delisted_coverage: YES but shallow: documentation-derived statement that history reaches the 1960s for actively trading securities and only 2007 for delisted securities.
sources.corporate_actions: yes (splits, dividends); terminal events UNKNOWN
sources.permanent_identifiers: Intrinio security_id, plus CIK/FIGI cross-reference
sources.adjustment_methodology: adjusted and unadjusted endpoints
sources.api_format: REST JSON, CSV bulk downloads
sources.licensing: per-feed subscription; commercial terms quote-based
sources.cost_category: UNKNOWN (pricing page is quote-driven; historical retail feeds were low thousands per year)
sources.cost_evidence: no price captured without signing up
sources.integration_complexity: low-medium
sources.caveats: 2007 is late but still earlier than our 2011 bar floor, so it would technically cover the replay window.

sources.name: Databento (US Equities)
sources.delisted_coverage: Partial and of the wrong kind: it is raw exchange market data replayed as-recorded, so a symbol that traded on a given day IS in that day's data, expired/retired instrument ids included. But it is not a curated security-master product and the public pages do not claim survivorship-bias-free equity histories.
sources.delisted_from: implicitly, whatever the captured feed contains
sources.earliest_date: '16+ years' claimed for US equities (start date not published on the pricing page)
sources.corporate_actions: sold as a SEPARATE corporate-actions product; the price feeds themselves are unadjusted by nature
sources.permanent_identifiers: instrument_id within a dataset plus a symbology service; not a cross-vendor permanent id
sources.adjustment_methodology: none -- as-traded only
sources.api_format: DBN binary, with CSV/JSON export; official clients are Python/C++/Rust (the Python client is not stdlib)
sources.licensing: notably liberal: most datasets may be redistributed internally or externally after 24 hours, per-dataset terms
sources.cost_evidence: pricing page as read 2026-09-21: Standard $199/mo, Plus $1,750/mo (annual), Unlimited $4,500/mo (annual), PLUS usage-based $/GB on top of any tier; $125 free credits. The usage component means the annual total is genuinely UNKNOWN until a data volume is chosen.
sources.integration_complexity: high: tick/MBO-shaped data is orders of magnitude larger than daily bars, and the natural client is a compiled library. Building daily bars for 7,000 dead names from raw feeds is an ingest project in itself, and the disk budget here is 11 GB.
sources.caveats: Wrong shape for this problem despite the attractive licence. Consider only if intraday work ever becomes a requirement.

sources.name: FirstRate Data
sources.delisted_coverage: YES and quantified: 16,303 US stock tickers of which over 7,000 are delisted, from January 2000.
sources.corporate_actions: NOT delivered as events -- only baked into the adjustment variants
sources.permanent_identifiers: none; ticker-keyed files
sources.adjustment_methodology: three variants shipped: unadjusted, split-only adjusted, split+dividend adjusted. Vendor notes unadjusted exists only for the 1-minute and 1-day timeframes -- 1-day is exactly what we need.
sources.api_format: zipped CSV bundles, one file per ticker, plus a simple download API
sources.licensing: UNKNOWN from the public pages; no redistribution/commercial statement was visible
sources.cost_evidence: vendor pages as read 2026-09-21 show bundle-level one-time purchases (a Russell 3000 intraday bundle listed at $399.95 on a third-party marketplace) with optional update subscriptions at $79.95-$99.95/mo. The exact price of the daily-stocks bundle was not displayed without going further into checkout, so treat the figure as a category, not a quote.
sources.integration_complexity: low-medium: CSV in a zip is ideal for a stdlib ingest; the cost is disk (unzip staging) and the absence of any identifier or event model
sources.caveats: A one-time purchase with no recurring dependency is attractive for a research replay that does not need to stay current. But with no permanent identifier and no corporate-action events, it solves the PRICE half and none of the IDENTITY half, and identity is where this store's invariants live.

sources.name: Exchange Data International (EDI) global stock prices
sources.delisted_coverage: YES per integrator documentation (delisted securities included, 2007-present)

sources.permanent_identifiers: EDI security ids plus ISIN/SEDOL
sources.adjustment_methodology: split- and dividend-adjusted per integrator docs; unadjusted UNKNOWN

sources.licensing: subscription, redistribution restricted
sources.cost_evidence: not published on the pages read

sources.corporate_actions: split/dividend columns in WIKI
sources.permanent_identifiers: none
sources.adjustment_methodology: adjusted columns alongside raw
sources.api_format: REST/CSV
sources.licensing: WIKI was public domain-ish; EOD is a paid feed

sources.name: OpenFIGI (Bloomberg)
sources.delisted_coverage: identifiers only -- NO PRICES. FIGIs are issued for instruments including ones that no longer trade, and the mapping API resolves ticker+exchange+date-less keys to a composite FIGI.
sources.corporate_actions: no
sources.permanent_identifiers: FIGI / composite FIGI / share-class FIGI -- genuinely permanent and free to use, the only free permanent identifier in this survey
sources.adjustment_methodology: n/a
sources.api_format: REST JSON, free API key, vendor states no daily/weekly/monthly limit
sources.licensing: free and openly usable; FIGI is an open standard
sources.cost_evidence: vendor page: 'The API is free to use without daily, weekly or monthly limitations.'
sources.integration_complexity: low
sources.caveats: Solves the identifier requirement and nothing else. Worth adopting regardless of which price decision is made, because a FIGI column in pit_listing would let any future vendor be joined without re-deriving identity.

sources.name: SEC EDGAR derived: Form 25 / 25-NSE + 8-K Item 3.01 + Form 15 (free)
sources.delisted_coverage: DATES AND REASONS, NEVER PRICES. Measured this survey: 25-NSE first appears in the EDGAR full index in 2006Q3 (328 filings; 2006Q1 and 2005Q2 have zero, consistent with the 2006 electronic-filing amendment), then runs 330-406 per quarter through 2025Q1. EDGAR full-text search reports >=10,000 hits (capped). All five dead issuers probed (Sears, Bed Bath & Beyond, Lehman, Circuit City, Toys R Us) expose BOTH a Form 25/25-NSE and an 8-K carrying item 3.01 in their submissions JSON.
sources.delisted_from: 2006 for exchange-filed 25-NSE; issuer 8-K Item 3.01 from 2004 (when the item was created); paper Form 25 earlier
sources.earliest_date: covers our entire replay window, which starts 2011-01-03 for bars and 2013-01-31 for peer sets
sources.corporate_actions: delisting notices, deregistration (Form 15), and merger disclosure in 8-K items 1.01/2.01 -- but no prices, no ratios unless parsed from text
sources.permanent_identifiers: CIK, which we already key on (pit_entity.cik)
sources.adjustment_methodology: n/a
sources.api_format: data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK##########.json exposes form + filingDate + an ITEMS field per 8-K, so item 3.01 is detectable without downloading the 8-K document itself; EDGAR full-index form.idx per quarter lists every 25-NSE
sources.licensing: public domain, no restriction, commercial use permitted
sources.cost_evidence: no charge; requires the ShafferFinEval UA and <=10 req/s
sources.integration_complexity: low: stdlib urllib + json, and pit_entity_exit already exists with exactly the right vocabulary (exit_date_source in {8k_item_301, form_25nse, last_volume_bar}, dereg_date kept separate with the comment 'Form 15. NEVER used as exit_date.')
sources.caveats: This resolves WHEN and WHY a company died, never WHAT THE FINAL PRICE WAS. Under owner rule 4 that is still valuable: it converts a silently-omitted name into an explicit OUTCOME_UNKNOWN with a dated terminal event.

sources.name: Nasdaq Trader symbol directory files (free)
sources.delisted_coverage: current state only. nasdaqlisted.txt and otherlisted.txt are today's universe; TradingSystemAddsDeletes.txt carries symbol, action (Add/Delete) and effective date, but the documentation does not indicate an archived history of past deletions.
sources.corporate_actions: no
sources.permanent_identifiers: no
sources.adjustment_methodology: n/a
sources.api_format: plain text files over FTP at ftp.nasdaqtrader.com/symboldirectory/
sources.licensing: free public files
sources.cost_evidence: no charge
sources.integration_complexity: low, but only useful going forward
sources.caveats: Useless retrospectively for 2011-2026 because we did not snapshot it. Worth snapshotting daily from now on -- it is the cheapest way to stop the bleeding for FUTURE delistings.

excluded.reason: anti-bot wall; scraping it would be circumvention. Not considered.

WRDS is an access route, not a source. It requires an institutional (university) subscription that an individual cannot buy, and its licences forbid commercial product use. Relevant only if the owner obtains an academic affiliation.

crash_prices_json.audit_verdict: THE PRIOR AUDIT HOLDS, and is if anything understated.

measured.null_keys_are_exactly_the_delisted_names: AVP = Avon Products, acquired by Natura January 2020. X = US Steel, acquired by Nippon Steel June 2025. Both are JSON null: the fetch returned nothing and the dead names carry no data at all.
measured.last_bar_dates: every one of the 41 ends 2026-08-14 or 2026-08-17
measured.back_adjustment_evidence: 1962 opening values of DIS 0.0566, KO 0.0445, JNJ 0.0600, IBM 1.4344 -- orders of magnitude below as-traded 1962 prices, i.e. auto_adjust back-adjusted, with every split and dividend since folded into the early history
measured.survivorship_smoking_gun: GM begins 2010-11-18, the post-bankruptcy successor's IPO. The old General Motors Corporation, which traded from 1916 to 2009 and went to zero, is absent, and the ticker GM silently resolves to a different company with the same three letters. This is the exact failure mode a permanent identifier prevents.

crash_prices_json.does_it_help: NO, not for survivorship. 43 hand-picked crash-era names, 41 of them survivors, 2 of them null, no terminal prices, back-adjusted only, foreign listings in local units (4 Tokyo names, LLOY.L in pence). It is a narrative illustration file for an essay about bubbles, not a price sample. It cannot repair the survivor-only sample and must not be merged into pit_price_bar.
crash_prices_json.one_thing_it_does_prove: It independently reproduces the Yahoo failure mode on a different machine and a different date: ask Yahoo for a dead company and you get null, not a final price.

sec_reconstruction_of_delisting_dates.verdict: YES -- delisting DATES and reasons are recoverable for free, for the whole replay window, without any price vendor.

measured.form_25nse_first_quarter_in_edgar: 2006Q3 (328 filings). 2005Q2 and 2006Q1 contain zero 25-NSE and only 107/129 old-style Form 25.
measured.edgar_full_text_search_total_25nse: >=10,000 (the API caps the reported total at 10,000, so the true count is higher; extrapolating ~350/quarter over ~82 quarters gives roughly 28,000 filings 2006-2026)
measured.dead_issuer_probe: 5 of 5 known-dead issuers (Sears Holdings 2018-10-15, Bed Bath & Beyond 2023-04-25, Lehman 2008-09-23, Circuit City 2008-10-30, Toys R Us 2005-07-27) expose an 8-K with item 3.01 AND a Form 25/25-NSE in data.sec.gov submissions
measured.cost_to_sweep_all_entities: 0.16 MB average per submissions JSON x 16,890 entities = ~2.71 GB streamed, retaining only extracted rows; at <=10 req/s that is ~28 minutes of wall clock
measured.already_scaffolded: pit_entity_exit exists with exit_date_source in {8k_item_301, form_25nse, last_volume_bar}, a separate dereg_date documented 'Form 15. NEVER used as exit_date.', and a no_exit_record quarantine flag. 7 rows are populated today, 2 of them honest quarantines.

sec_reconstruction_of_delisting_dates.what_it_cannot_do: It cannot produce a terminal price, a recovery value, or an exchange ratio without parsing the merger 8-K text, and it must not be used to infer one. A Form 25 proves the security stopped trading on that exchange; it does not prove the shareholder received zero, and an OTC stub often kept trading for years afterwards (BBBYQ, SHLDQ, LEHMQ all did).
sec_reconstruction_of_delisting_dates.what_it_is_worth: It converts a silently missing name into a dated, sourced OUTCOME_UNKNOWN. Under owner rule 4 and rule 6 that is the difference between an honest gap and survivorship bias.

local_store_gap.reading: 8,655 entities that plainly stopped filing -- the overwhelming majority of the dead -- have no price line at all. pit_listing_status already records 1,390 entities as LISTING_UNRESOLVED with reason price_series_gate_failed against 2,542 resolved.

recommendation.decision: NO PAID SOURCE YET. Do the free half first, then buy exactly one thing and only after a sample test.
steps: 1. FREE, DO NOW: sweep data.sec.gov submissions for every entity and populate pit_entity_exit from Form 25/25-NSE and 8-K item 3.01. ~2.71 GB streamed, ~28 minutes at 10 req/s, retains only small rows. This ends silent omission: every dead peer gets a dated, sourced exit and an explicit OUTCOME_UNKNOWN.
2. FREE, DO NOW: add a FIGI column via OpenFIGI so any future vendor joins on a permanent identifier instead of a ticker.
3. FREE, DO NOW: start snapshotting the Nasdaq Trader symbol directory daily so future delistings are never lost the way 2011-2026 were.
4. FREE, DO NOW: keep labelling every price-derived result SURVIVOR_ONLY_DIAGNOSTIC. Steps 1-3 do not change that; they make the gap explicit rather than invisible.

5. THEN, IF A PAID SOURCE IS STILL WANTED: buy Sharadar SEP+TICKERS+ACTIONS, and only it. It is the only candidate that satisfies all four hard requirements at a non-institutional cost: delisted included by design, discrete corporate-action events, a permanent identifier (permaticker), and closeunadj for pre-split share counts. Before paying, ask for or sample-test 20 known 2013-2023 delistings from our own pit_entity_exit and confirm the series runs to the delisting date.

6. DO NOT buy Norgate despite the best coverage-per-dollar ($630/yr, 25,222 delisted, 1990+): it exposes no corporate-action events, its delivery path is a Windows updater plus a pandas-dependent Python package that the stdlib-only rule forbids, and a full delisted backfill at its scale (~7.7 GB) does not fit in 11 GB of free disk.

7. DO NOT buy CRSP, Bloomberg, LSEG, FactSet or Capital IQ. CRSP is the correct answer to the research question and the wrong answer to this budget: institutional-negotiated, no self-serve path, and academic access requires an institution.
recommendation.why_not_yet: A paid feed bought today would be poured into an architecture that cannot yet say which names are missing. The SEC sweep costs nothing, is measured and feasible, and produces the list of dead names a vendor would then be asked to price. Buying first would also invite the very thing the owner forbade: a tempting new return sample that still answers a different question from the one asked.
recommendation.what_would_change_this: If the sample test in step 5 shows Sharadar's dead tail is complete to the delisting date for our own dead peers, the low-hundreds-to-low-thousands annual cost is justified and should be paid. If a commercial product is ever distributed, the licence question moves to the front: Sharadar professional and Polygon business tiers permit it; Tiingo's cheap tier explicitly does not.
